Oral Questions
research or political discussion of pornography. Would the Minister agree that these are sensible safeguards, and give a commitment to introduce them at the same time as the provisions he has already put into the draft legislation?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I do thank the Hon. Member for notice of her question. 1 am, in any event, aware of the representations of the Canadian Association of University Teachers. I am not aware of any history of persecution by Attorneys General in their administration of the legislation which would justify changing the character of the existing Section to put the onus entirely on the Crown. I really do not see why there should be any need at this time for a change of that kind to give a broader protection than now exists, because the existing Section seems to be quite adequate.

Madam Speaker, the existing provision refers to the public good but is not as specific, I trust the Minister will realize, as what is being proposed, which says quite specifically serious artistic, scientific, medical, literary or political value. It also gives some other specifications about use in universities and so forth.

We do not want new vigorous laws to go overboard and in the wrong direction. The CAUT proposal would be a means of giving some equilibrium to the law. The new law would be tough, but it would be directed to real pornography and could not be used as an excuse for a new witch-hunt of people like D. H. Lawrence or own Margaret Laurence.

The House resumed consideration of Bill C-155, an Act to facilitate the transportation, shipping and handling of western grain and to amend certain Acts in consequence thereof, as
Western Grain Transportation Act
reported (with amendments) from the Standing Committee on Transport; and Motions Nos. 24, 25, 26 and 29 (Mr. Benjamin) and Motion No. 27 (Mr. Gustafson).

Madam Speaker, 1 am pleased to stand and participate in the debate on Motion No.
27 which deals with representation on the Senior Grain Transportation Committee. 1 am somewhat surprised that the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) had so little to say on the matter of the statutory Crow rate. I believe his speech consisted of less than a couple of lines.
I was also surprised that Government Members were not here for two hours and delayed debate on this Bill this morning.
Since this is a historical piece of legislation with which we are dealing and because representation on the Transportation Committee is so important, I believe it is fair to say that the farmers in western Canada are very concerned about who is represented. 1 believe if one studied the action and direction which the Progressive Conservative Party has taken with this Bill, one will find that we have constantly recommended producer representation on the Transportation Committee. While certain Members have said that the Conservatives had taken one position then and another position now, 1 suggest that nothing is further from the truth. I have reread some of the speeches made by the Hon. Member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) and also went as far as to read some of mine. I want to suggest that since the outset of debate on Bill C-155 this spring, which has gone on for some time, we have constantly defended the position of the primary producer and the farmer.
The statutory Crow rate was originally established so that produce could be delivered to the open water ports of this country which, in most cases, are more than 1,000 miles away. It was most important that the agreements which were reached at that time would allow the producers the right to believe that their products would get to the markets of the world, and it is our position that this Bill in no way would obstruct the rights and the privileges of the producer to produce his grain and realize a fair return for his production.
In dealing with Motion No. 27 in particular, 1 want to go back to the original proposal that was put forward and amended by the Hon. Member for Kindersley-Lloydminster (Mr. McKnight). In keeping with the direction that our Party has taken, it was suggested that there should first be a producer representation of one from the Province of Alberta, two from the Province of Saskatchewan due to its high production of grain as compared to Alberta and Manitoba, and one producer from the Province of Manitoba. It was the Hon. Member for Kindersley-Lloydminster, on behalf of the Progressive Conservative Party, who implemented this on behalf of the producers.
Our reason for moving Motion No. 27 is that we believe it is important that there be equal representation from producer elevators and grain line companies. Basically, this motion states that there will be three members from the grain line
COMMONS DEBATES__________________________________September 29, 1983
Western Grain Transportation Act companies and three representatives from the Pools, which are the Alberta Pool, Saskatchewan Pool and Manitoba Pool. Once again, our Party has mapped out a direction that is fair and equitable in respect of the Senior Grain Transportation Committee.
Since this Committee will play a very important role in directing the activities of transportation and making suggestions to the council, it is most important that it has fair representation. 1 also suggest in regard to the smaller grain companies that they have representation according to Clause 3(e)(ii). The smaller companies such as Parrish Heimbecker, Weyburn Terminal and others will have the right to elect one member to represent them on the board.
I want to re-emphasize the importance of having broad representation and producer representation. If the Government has made one major mistake in the Bill, if the former Minister has made one major mistake-one of several, 1 believe-and the Minister who was in charge before him has made a mistake, it is that they have not investigated the situation of the primary producer. They have not researched the problems that the producer faces and do not realize that the producers are incapable of meeting the increased freight rates that they will be expected to pay. I suggest that is the greatest mistake which has been made in Bill C-155. Producer representation is the most important element in this Bill.
The Hon. Member for Vegreville and the Conservative Party have justifiably made great attempts to make sure that one producer is not played against another. That is exactly what the Government has done and we have tried in every way possible, through our amendments, to make sure that that kind of obstruction does not exist.
If the prairie producer is not considered when we deal with this or any other clause of the Bill, our country faces a very serious situation. 1 want to draw a comparison because I think it is helpful.
The Government, through its national energy policy, took action while not understanding that it was putting Canadians out of work and putting the primary producer in the oil fields of western Canada out of business. The Government chose to buy oil from Mexico. The Canadian oil fields were shut down and put out of business. I am glad the Minister is here. 1 want to say to him that if the primary producers in agriculture are put out of business because they cannot meet the costs, and research shows that the costs to the primary producer are high, the impact will be great. The impact of the national energy policy will be small in comparison to the impact it will have on agriculture throughout this country.
This and other amendments we have put forward protect the primary producer. They are most important. We ask the Government to accept these amendments in the interests of the primary producer.
1 see I have about half a minute remaining, Mr. Speaker, so let me say that if the farmers are to be represented, it will be the Progressive Conservatives who represent the interests of
the farmer and the primary producer. I have said that in the House, in my riding and across southern Saskatchewan. It is important that they be represented. That is no more important than Motion No. 27 which puts the producer into a position of responsibility and a position where the producer has some input with the Minister in charge.

Mr. Speaker, I will be very brief. Motion No. 27, of course, would be impossible unless Motion No. 26 was passed. Sub-clause 3(e) states, "not more than 11 other Members", and the three Members cannot be increased to six other Members without increasing the 11 to 14, a move which 1 shall oppose for a number of reasons.
First, I have always believed that the committee is too large to be functional. It is very difficult to get advice from a committee with that many members. One would probably get conflicting advice all down the line. My second reason for opposing it is that Clause 3 as it is now written is amended from the original clause in the Bill by an amendment put forward by the Progressive Conservative Party in the committee and accepted by the committee. I intend to stand by the proposal adopted by the committee.

Mr. Speaker, I was very interested to hear the Hon. Member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gustafson) talk about the Conservative Party, the co-operative movement, and how they are supporting farmers in the Province of Saskatchewan. He has moved Motion No. 27 which would, in effect, have three Members on the Senior Grain Transportation Committee which is referred to in the Bill.
When the Bill was originally drafted, the three prairie Wheat Pools were to have three committee members on the Senior Grain Transportation Committee. During the summer, the Conservative Party, in a blatant attack upon the Wheat Pools and co-operative movement of this country, introduced an amendment-I believe it was introduced by the Hon.
Member for Kindersley-Lloydminster (Mr. McKnight)__________
which reduced the number of committee members from three to one. Now we have the Member for Assiniboia saying in the House that they made a serious mistake. Once again they are changing their mind. It is like the Leader of the Conservative Party who is on both sides of every single issue that comes up in the House, that is when he has the courage to come into the House. During the summer, the Conservative Party said that the Wheat Pool should not have three members on the committee. Their amendment was passed, supported by the Liberal Party, and now the Member for Assiniboia contradicts his own Party, once again saying that the Wheat Pool should have three members on this committee. That shows the confusion there is in that Party over the Bill now before the House. It shows that they do not know where they stand on the important issue of the Crow rate as it affects western Canadian farmers.
I am concerned also about where they stand on a number of other motions before the House. We are not debating just this motion. By the way, Motion No. 27, moved by the Hon.

September 29, 1983
Member for Assiniboia, is exactly the same as the motion that was put on the Order Paper by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin), that is, Motion No. 26.
My colleague from Regina West was the only person in the committee who voted to have three Wheat Pool members on the committee. The Conservative Party voted against it. He is the Member who led the attack on behalf of the Wheat Pools, which market the majority of grain in my Province. He was the only Member who stood up and defended them against the combined forces of the Liberal and Conservative Parties.
He is the only one who showed up. We never saw you there.

We only have one Member on that committee. That Member was at the committee throughout the summer. We also had one alternate and we made sure he was there at every hearing. The Conservative Party often went day after day after day without its full delegation of representatives on the committee or their full delegation of alternates. Where were they?

Mr. Speaker, 1 rise on a point of order. 1 hate to do this, but 1 am not going to sit here and listen to the Hon. Member attack Members who spent a great deal of time this past summer on the committee. What the Hon. Member just said is patently not true. The Conservative Party was fully represented there at all times.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The Hon. Member for Northumberland-Miramichi (Mr. Dionne) may agree or disagree with the remarks made by the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom), but that is basically a matter for debate. Matters like that should not be raised under the guise of points of order.

It is very interesting to see the Liberal Party jump to the defence of the Conservative Party once again. I guess it shows the true alliance in this country. That is why when the motion was moved last summer reducing the number of Wheat Pool representatives from three to one, the Liberal Party supported that Conservative amendment. It shows who are the true friends of the farmer.
The other motion that is important here is Motion No. 24, moved by the Hon. Member for Regina West. That motion would delete the word "co-operative" in Clause 3 of the Bill. This is another indication of a blatant Conservative attack on co-operatives and the United Grain Growers. It makes it impossible for wheat pool directors, officers or committee members of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool, Manitoba Wheat Pool, Alberta Wheat Pool, or UGG to be members of the Senior Grain Transportation Committee.
1 do not know whether the Conservative Party believes in democracy. However, this kind of clause in the Bill virtually eliminates thousands and thousands of ordinary farmers in all three prairie Provinces from running for democratic office and being a member of the Senior Grain Transportation Commit-
Western Grain Transportation Act tee. In my riding-and I am sure the same is true in the riding of Assiniboia-there are hundreds of ordinary farmers who are Wheat Pool Committee men. They work for the Canadian Wheat Pool or for United Grain Growers. With Clause 3 of the Bill in effect there is no way they could seek office.
Another point is that we have taken the time and trouble to obtain a legal opinion. We were told by a lawyer that this meant that ordinary Wheat Pool Committee men or farmers who are out there trying to work for the Wheat Pool would not be eligible to run for office. Yet the Conservative Party would eliminate thousands of ordinary farmers in my Province from the democratic process. 1 believe in freedom, I believe in liberty, and 1 believe in the right of every man and woman to seek elected office. 1 believe in true democracy and in economic democracy. It makes me very angry as a Member of Parliament to see hundreds of my friends in my constituency being excluded from the democratic rights they should enjoy by the Conservative Party.
And supported by the Liberals.

Unfortunately, their leaders, such as Ronald Reagan and Margaret Thatcher, talk about freedom and democracy, freedom and democracy if one is wealthy and rich, freedom and democracy for the elite. When it comes to ordinary citizens or farmers in Kamsack, Canora, Church-bridge, Melville or Ituna in my riding, that same Party will deny them the right to be members of the Senior Grain Transportation Committee. I cannot understand it. 1 would be very interested in knowing whether or not there would be any support whatsoever for that among Canadians. 1 am absolutely sure that there would not be.
They are not bad guys, just misled.

I believe I hear the Hon. Member for Leth-bridge-Foothills (Mr. Thacker) making utterances from his seat. I would be very interested in hearing him rise in the House to defend the stand of the Conservative Party that ordinary Wheat Pool Committee men cannot seek office on this Senior Grain Transportation Committee. 1 would be very interested in seeing him rise to make an undemocratic speech. Also 1 am interested in ensuring that all farmers in the prairie Provinces know where the Conservative Party really stands. It is interested in giving the private grain trade seats on that committee. It is interested in giving the railways seats on that committee.
1 see the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) is present today. He must be embarrassed because his face is turning the same colour as his jacket. He must be embarrassed to know that his Party is supporting a clause in the Bill which is undemocratic. It stands against freedom. His Party moved that particular clause. Members of that Party are denying basic rights to ordinary men and women. It is something which goes back to the nineteenth century and tells us where the Conservative Party really stands.

September 29, 1983
Western Grain Transportation Act
One of the motives for its amendment is that it is attacking the Wheat Pool movement and the United Grain Growers. It is defending its friends in the private grain trade and in the private grain exchange. The co-operative movement in Canada has been very important. The people who built the wheat pools, the co-operatives and the credit unions made a tremendous contribution to the country. As I travel throughout my riding I see wheat pool elevators in village after village, town after town. Those people want to be treated fairly and squarely. They want at least three members on the Committee. They do not want the membership reduced to one, as the Conservative Party would like it. Also they want to ensure that ordinary grassroot farmers have a chance to be members of that committee, not just bureaucrats, Government officials and the corporate elite which the Conservative Party would like to see running the affairs of the country.
I do not apologize for standing up for ordinary citizens in the House of Commons. It is very interesting to see how the Conservative Party, when push comes to shove, will not stand up for ordinary Canadian citizens. I am very shocked that several of my friends in that Party, who I know believe in democracy, fair trade and equal treatment, will sit on their hind-ends and allow their Party leadership to get away with this nonsense and discrimination against western Canadians and ordinary farmers in my constituency and indeed right across the land.

Mr. Speaker, I find it rather strange that Members of the New Democratic Party started out in this debate by saying that they would do everything in their power to kill the Bill and now they are making various proposals and deals with the Government in an attempt to get some parts of it through. That was the essence of their press release and their questions today. If there is any caving in, it seems to be coming from the NDP.
I rise in support of Motion No. 27 presented by the Hon. Member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gustafson). The motion would establish a representation on the Senior Grain Transportation Committee from the primary elevator system in Canada. In part it reads:
-six members, each representing one of the six largest primary elevator licensees in Canada as prescribed by regulations made by the Governor in Council, and determined on the basis of elevator receipts and cash purchase tickets.
This would mean that each of the three prairie pools would have one representative, United Grain Growers would have a representative, Pioneer would have a representative, as would Cargill.
The Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) moved two of the motions we are now debating. In Motion No. 25 he proposes five members, and then as a safety valve he proposes six members in Motion No. 26. Motion 24 is a perfectly logical and reasonable amendment. I certainly want to support it. It is consistent with the proposition of fairness, and consistent particularly with our major thrust in ensuring that producers have adequate representation on the Senior Grain Transportation Committee and in ensuring that the producers' interest is incorporated in the Bill.
One of the many deficiencies in the Bill is the lack of any mention of producer interest and the requirement to maximize returns to the producer. We have incorporated that into several clauses of the Bill as one of the primary obligations of the Senior Grain Transportation Committee as well as the Grain Transportation Agency Administrator. It is important to recognize the welfare of the producer. We are really setting up a new grain handling and transportation system and a new grain handling and transportation administration. We were appalled by the fact that there was hardly a mention of the producer. We sought to incorporate that in the Bill. The thrust of our amendments to the Senior Grain Transportation Committee concerns grassroot producers who are not necessarily tied into any grain handling company, grain handling system or co-operative.
We think that the pools can adequately maintain representation on these kinds of organizations through their administration and management, but we thought it was very important to include individual producers whose sole aim, objective and purpose in life is to produce grain. It is important to have them there functioning and representing the interest of the producer, not the interests of grain elevators or any other association.
The Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) became excited and indicated that the Conservatives were trying to exclude ordinary producers. The fact of the matter is that we are doing just the opposite. We are trying to include ordinary producers and to ensure that ordinary producers who have no other vested interest, have an opportunity to sit down with the Senior Grain Transportation Committee. That committee will be attended by the Chairman of the Canadian Wheat Board, the Chairman of the Canadian Grain Commission, representatives of the railways and representatives of the grain elevator companies so that they can say, "Look, guys, there is a problem here," and so that they can speak directly to the railroads, so that they can speak directly to the Chairman of the Canadian Grain Commission and the Chief Commissioner of the Canadian Wheat Board. We think that that is very important.
The Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville has become very excited when talking about attendance of Conservative Members. This committee travelled across western Canada and visited his home Province. He did not even attend the hearings in the Province of Saskatchewan. Out of the 66 meetings that this committee held, the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville attended only one meeting. That only goes to show his interest in the Bill and his interest in the welfare of the producers. Yet he stands here today and pontificates and chastises Conservative Members and Liberal Members.
I am pleased that the chairman of the committee stood up in defence of all Hon. Members who worked very hard and very diligently and for long hours to try to dissect each and every clause of the Bill and to try to seek out solutions. There
September 29, 1983

certainly were differences of opinion, and there will be still more as the Bill proceeds, but the fact of the matter is that the Members worked very hard. I take violent exception to the fact that the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville chastised us after attending only one committee hearing.
1 should add, Mr. Speaker, that the chairman of the committee was very generous. Whether an Hon. Member was a member of the committee or whether he just attended as an observer, the chairman allowed all Members to participate. He was very generous with the committee s time, and certainly when we travelled to Regina, Edmonton, and Winnipeg, any Member who was located in the area had the opportunity to sit in on the committee hearings and to participate in any way, shape or form excepting only for the opportunity to vote. 1 commend him for it, and I think as a result of that, the committee hearing process was much better.
1 take violent exception to the fact that a Member such as the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville can come to the House in such an excited state and try to suggest that we as members of the committee were attempting to exclude the primary producer when the opposite is the fact.
We moved a motion, Mr. Speaker, that would incorporate four producer members into the Senior Grain Transportation Committee. I guess the difference between the position taken by Members of the Conservative Party and the position taken by representatives of the pools was the fact that pools collectively wanted to exclude the producers. We do not know why the representatives from the pools wanted that. They made the point that they wanted to exclude the producers. Rather than having three producer members as originally called for in the Bill, they suggested that that be deleted and that the Chairman of the Wheat Board Advisory Committee and the Chairman of the Livestock Feed Board Advisory Committee represent the producers. We found that totally unsatisfactory and, as a result, we moved an amendment which allowed four grain producers to be members of the board, two from the Province of Saskatchewan and one each from the Provinces of Alberta and Manitoba.
In addition, we moved another amendment which allowed for a feed grain producer to be represented on this committee. We also made other changes to the Senior Grain Transportation Committee by allowing for representation from the trucking industry. When we are talking theoretically about the movement of grain, we must remember that every bushel of grain that moves travels by truck. The trucking industry is an important component of the whole grain moving system.
In terms of enlarging the objectives and the terms of reference of the Senior Grain Transportation Committee, we have endeavoured to have the members of that committee commit themselves in their duties and obligations to the principles of maximizing the returns to producers and representing the best interests of the producers. We endeavoured to do the same regarding the terms of reference of the Grain Transport Administrator and we think that that is a step in the right direction because, throughout the course of our hearings, we were told time and time again that the producers' interests
Western Grain Transportation Act were not clearly enunciated in the Bill, and that is what we wanted to change.
1 would like to speak briefly to Motion No. 29. Hon. Members of the New Democratic Party want to stop the railways from having a seat on the Senior Grain Transportation Committee. How absurd could they be, Mr. Speaker? The producers want to get their hands on the representatives of the railroad at committee. That is where the decision-making process, the communications process and the entire co-ordination and consultation process should take place.
I find the position taken by Members of the NDP to be absolutely ludicrous and absolutely absurd. In my opinion, the real action will take place at committee, because I can see producers who have been shortchanged by improper allocation of cars, shortage of cars or lack of service tangling with the railroads there. I can see them tangling with the Chief Commissioner of the Canadian Wheat Board and the member from the Canadian Grain Commission, but it is important to have the railway representatives present because if they are not at the table, then this committee will be worthless. 1 say to you, Mr. Speaker, that I hope the Government will see fit to support Motion No. 27 and reject Motion No. 29.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words respecting Motion No. 27 which was so excellently moved by my friend, the Hon. Member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gustafson), it appears to me that the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) either did not listen when the Hon. Member was speaking or did not bother reading the amendment, because the allegations he made are simply unfounded. They are not right. That is not what the Hon. Member for Assiniboia said at all. As a matter of fact, the words of the Hon. Member for Assiniboia were fair and just. Fairness and justice is what we want and what our people and our farmers want.
I would ask the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville if it is fair and just for a group that handles 20 per cent of the grain in western Canada to be entitled to membership on the committee. He suggests that we designate members according to the organization. The Hon. Member for Assiniboia is suggesting that we designate members in accordance with the amount of business done. That is sensible and 1 am sure every farmer in the country would support that. It makes sense.
As a matter of fact, I received a phone call from a member of the Alberta Wheat Pool recently. He said: "This isn't fair at all. We handle far more grain than another company and we have many, many more elevators. But our representation isn't anything near what it should be. We should have more than one representative for the three prairie Provinces." 1 agree with that. I am not going to argue the case for the Alberta Wheat Pool or the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool or the Manitoba Wheat Pool. 1 am arguing the case for the farmer who is entitled to fair representation.
If a large percentage of farmers take their grain to the Alberta Wheat Pool, that indicates that there should be more representation from the pools than from independent compa-

September 29, 1983
Western Grain Transportation Act nies, and vice versa. If farmers take 50 per cent of their grain to an independent company, are we to leave that company out because it does not happen to be one of the big boys with big elevators? That is what the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Mel-ville is suggesting. He is suggesting that we are to designate them. I say that that is offering special favours and special privileges and we are against special privileges. We want to be fair to every individual farmer in the country. This amendment is fair to every individual farmer in the country.
The Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville talked about killing the Bill. He is more concerned with killing the Conservative Party because he is frightened that, day by day, he is getting closer to losing his seat.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I wonder if it is in order to distort what I said. It was Members of the Conservative Party who moved the motion to reduce the Wheat Pool representation from three to one. They did it.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. That is hardly a point of order. That is debate. Hon. Members will have the opportunity to contribute additonal remarks to the debate later on. The Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) has the floor.

Mr. Speaker, this is the kind of misrepresentation which the Hon. Member tries to make continually. He is not getting through to the people of western Canada because he is not telling the truth. This Party is not trying to reduce the membership of any particular organization. We want to have representation according to the way individual farmers deal with them. That is the basis of it. If ten farmers take their wheat to one pool and 100 farmers take it to another, why should we insist on one having ten members and the other one maybe no members?
The Hon. Member for Assiniboia tries to be fair but, by misrepresentation, the Member from the NDP tries to hide the facts. The resolution of the Hon. Member for Assiniboia calls for six members-the original motion says three-each representing one of the six largest primary elevator licencees in Canada as prescribed by regulations made by the Governor in Council and determined on the basis of elevator receipts and cash purchase tickets. The interpretation given by the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville is completely different from that.
I want the farmers in my riding to know what the Conservative Party is doing. We do not stand for special privilege. We want the farmer to have a fair show, whether he has five cents in his pocket, whether he has 1,000 hogs, whether he has five elevators or whether he is a quarter-section farmer, he is an individual, a Canadian and is entitled to representation. When the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville tries to mislead the House, we have to be suspicious of his motive.
1 support the amendment and I will be prepared to stand anywhere in Canada and fight for the principle. All too often I have seen the big shots get in where they have a vested interest
instead of the people who go in objectively for the good of the country, not for their own pocketbook. That is what we want in Canada and that is what the Hon. Member for Assiniboia is fighting for. That is what his motion says in black and white for anyone to read. The trouble is that the NDP Members do not read anything unless they like it. If it is socialistic, they will read it.
The Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville said he had legal opinion. I would like to know where he got that legal opinion because I have legal opinion that is completely different. The man who gave me the legal opinion will stand head and shoulders above any solicitor his Party can put forward. If he wants to name his legal opinion, I will be glad to name mine.
Let us forget the legal opinion for a moment and get down to the common sense of the ordinary, every day farmer. Let each of them interpret Clause 3(d) of the Bill. They are not illiterate. The clause deals with the membership of the Senior Grain Transportation Committee as follows:
Four members who are active grain producers currently holding a Canadian Wheat Board permit book-
They have to be growing wheat and selling it to an elevator and have a Canadian Wheat Board permit book. It goes on:
-and who, in the opinion of the Minister, have been duly elected as representatives of grain producers-
Not appointed but elected, Mr. Speaker:
-one representing the producers of Manitoba, two representing the producers of Saskatchewan and one representing the producers of Alberta, and who, at the time of their election, and for the duration of their service as members of the Committee are not nominees, officers, directors, agents or representatives of any corporation-
This is not one from a corporation that has a vested interest, or a co-operative that has a vested interest or a business that has a vested interest. The NDP Members would leave all of them in, however, except the co-operatives. They would delete co-operatives but apparently all the others are fine with them. Why should there be a special privilege for the co-operatives?
I deal with co-operatives because I like their business, but they have never asked for a special privilege and I am not going to give them a special privilege. They will take their share along with everyone else.
The Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville indicated that an individual farmer would not get on the board, but that is who we want on the board, Mr. Speaker, not someone with a vested interest or someone who holds a high position in some agency or corporation or co-operative. We want the ordinary, every day farmer who will deal with things objectively. My hon. friends should take this back to their lawyer and tell him to read it. It does not bar the individual farmer, it perpetuates him. It gives us a chance to get a fresh, net opinion from the farmer fighting for a livelihood, not the rich, wealthy and special people.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak on the amendment to this Bill that would provide for farmers to be members of the Senior Grain Transportation Committee. I submit that the amendment ought to be accepted if for no other reason than that the history of the Crow rate
September 29, 1983

relates to the movement of grain. From its inception, this legislation was directed toward producers. For as long as the Crow rate has been in existence, there has been an intention to serve producers of the country. It only makes sense that when changes are made to the legislation, its fundamental purpose must be kept in mind. And the fundamental reason for the Crow rate originally was for the movement of grain in western Canada.
There are those who argue that we would deny representation to Wheat Pools, but it should be remembered that in the original draft of the legislation there was an opportunity for farmer-producer representation. It was the Wheat Pools, in their own interest, which took the view that they should be represented and not the producer. The Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) asked why we should single out the co-operatives for attention when it comes to having vested interests. How can we say that among all grain traders only they should be represented? Is there any reason that we should single them out for that privilege, among all grain traders?
I see I have the ear of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Axworthy). I would ask him if it is not obvious that the purpose of grain companies is to buy and sell grain and that this leads to the export of grain? Is it not also obviously the case that producers may do other things with grain than export it, particularly in Alberta where 47 per cent of grain grown is what we call "value added"? It goes into the production of poultry, pork, beef, or is in some other way used for some purpose other than being sold as whole grain. Those producers, who represent virtually one half of the agricultural income of Alberta, surely ought to have some say as opposed to those whose only objective is the export of grain. Those who are members only of a pool organization will reflect a perspective which is primarily self-serving, and that perspective will mean that grain will move from the Province without value added. I hear a little heckle coming to me from the New Democratic Party to my extreme left, whose Hon. Members, Mr. Speaker, are very pink and very ill read. Since that Hon. Member comes from the Province of Saskatchewan, he ought also to be aware enough of western agriculture to know that while he may be arguing his individual point, the truth of the prairies is that we are not homogeneous, and we ought not to be.
One of the great challenges which comes often from the Government side on this question is that the prairie people cannot get their act together. I hope we do not because our acts are in fact different. Saskatchewan exports almost 85 per cent of what it grows. In Alberta, a sister and neighbouring Province, virtually half of the grain grown is feed grain. Our producers have a different purpose from that of those who belong to grain companies whose first priority is to export. I submit, Sir, that it is counter to prairie production to say that it ought to be a grain company which sits on the Senior Grain Transportation Committee when in fact it is producers, for whom this Bill was designed originally, and for historic reasons who should continue to be the representatives from this day forth. This Bill is intended for the producers of western
Western Grain Transportation Act
Canada, and there is a variance in what Alberta and Saskatchewan do with their production. This variance can only be expressed with adequate producer representation.
I believe that the Hon. Member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gustafson) has done western Canada a great service by submitting that it should be those with the particular mental bent only to buy and sell grain and little else who should be removed by method of amendment in order to allow producers a variety of representation on a board which is sensitive to the needs of western Canada. A challenge was put forward by the Hon. Member for Bow River. How can the Government possibly select one set of grain traders and say that they are to be the privileged few is a question which absolutely demands an answer. We cannot pick out a grain company and stamp that across the three prairie Provinces, and say that it is privileged above all other companies, without any system of vote or any system of determining how it gets there. The Government surely cannot set up a committee which will have the power that this one will and not allow for some kind of input from the producers.
You will note, Mr. Speaker, that the Hon. Member for Mount St. Helen's is over here blowing his top again. He is a Member of the NDP and will probably not have the courage to speak himself, but he will stand here and shoot off steam and blow off ash as he always does. He sits over here and hollers through my microphone. I challenge him. He has a chance to rise and speak. We will allow him to do that any time that I sit down.
I would like to read into the record what the Province of Alberta, in its official submission, had to say with regard to this question of the Senior Grain Transportation Committee. It said this:
The Senior Grain Transportation Committee should be restructured so that a majority of the members represent Western farmers and are free of vested interest in the grain handling/transportation system.
In short, Mr. Speaker, what I am saying is that that is the official position of the Province of Alberta. The submission goes on to read as follows:
The grain farmer who has the responsibility to pay future cost increases is not adequately represented. The Crown is well represented through the Canadian Wheat Board, Canadian Grain Commission and the Administrator: the trade interests are covered through their appointed representatives, the railways' interests through their representatives but direct grain farmer representation is restricted to 3 out of the total 21 memberships.
What we find is that the Province of Alberta, as a provincial Government, stands opposed to the position of this Government. It would favour the amendment presented by the Hon. Member for Assiniboia. I feel it is important that I read into the record the position of the Alberta Wheat Pool. I quote directly as follows:
The Pools submit that representation on the Senior Grain Transportation Committee should be composed of those parties having a significant interest in and a direct responsibility for the transportation of western grain. This is considered desirable as it is anticipated that the Senior Grain Transportation Committee will be involved in significant grain transportation matters affecting Western Canada.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I appreciate the fact that the House has extended extra time. I would not want to take very much time but that the point I have been making hangs in limbo if I do not add some words to the quote I just read.
What the pools are saying in essence is that this is a transportation matter and it is only a transportation matter. The original debates, as they related to the Crow rate, back in the earlier history of this country, clearly showed that the establishment of a Crow rate was not purely a transportation matter, and in western Canada today it is not believed to be purely a transportation matter. This, Sir, is an economic development matter. If it were only a transportation question, as the pools are trying to submit that it is, their argument might be a more viable one.
The question is which way the economy of western Canada, and in turn the whole of Canada, is better served. I submit for your consideration, Mr. Speaker, and through you to the Minister, that the economy of western Canada is much better served if the members of that committee, which will have some considerable power, reflect the interests of those who are the growers of grains and the users of grains. We cannot conclude, Sir, that those who are intermediate to the process of bying and selling grain can be guaranteed to have the best interests of the growers always at heart. They have a vested interest. We would be fools to believe otherwise.
I submit in conclusion, Sir, that the Hon. Member for Assiniboia has presented an amendment which commands that we lend an ear and be respectful to the producers of this country, consistent with our history, with the fact that the principle of this Bill is to serve producers, and consistent with the fact that this is an economic initiative, not just a transportation initiative.
Now is your chance to speak.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Crowfoot (Mr. Malone) said that now it is my chance to speak. I do not know what he is getting at. Perhaps he is alluding to one of the Members who was standing behind me and shouting at him occasionally during his speech. He may have thought it was me, but it was not.
There are a number of things which have come up in this part of the debate, and what we are looking at is some amendments to set up the membership of the Senior Grain Transportation Committee as it will be called under the new legislation. What we have seen in the debate so far, particularly from my friends to the right, is a fair bit of misunderstanding, to put it charitably, and a lack of information as to what
actually went on to get us to where we are. I would like to put on the record what the process was from the time the original Bill was put before committee, what it said, and what happened to it in committee. Apparently the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor), in particular, is quite ignorant of what went on in committee.
The original Bill had the precise same wording as the amendment proposed by the Hon. Member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gustafson). But that was not good enough for the Conservative Members on the committee, so they got together with their friends across the way and proposed an amendment to that portion of the Bill, Clause 3, which we now see before us here today. That is a Conservative amendment proposed on September 1 at 9.40 in the morning by the Hon. Member for Kindersley-Lloydminster (Mr. McKnight). It is word for word exactly what he proposed, with one change. The Hon. Member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers) came in at 11.40 a.m. and proposed an amendment to the amendment, which was also incorporated in the Bill, and that is what we have here now. It was supported by the Liberals. The vote in each case was Liberals and Conservatives against the one lone New Democrat who sits on the committee.
In the course of the amendment by our good friend, the Hon. Member for Red Deer, the various organizations were named. Great issue has been taken with that by two or three previous speakers, but it was not until the Hon. Member moved his amendment that we were told who those committee members would represent. We were told very clearly that there would be one representative of the Canadian Co-operative Wheat Producers Organization, which is the umbrella organization for the three prairie pools; one member representing United Grain Growers Limited, and one member representing the two largest privately owned primary elevator companies. So it was the Hon. Member for Red Deer who put names on who would sit for whom. It was the Conservatives who changed the Bill as it was written and to which we are now proposing to return by the motion of the Hon. Member for Assiniboia; they changed it themselves. It was set up to provide a certain amount of equity, or the possibility of it. By having the six members you can see it would be possible to have at least one member representing each of the three prairie pools which collectively handle a little over 60 per cent of the grain in prairie Canada. The other two or three members could have been divided among the private grain companies and the United Grain Growers. They were not satisfied just to reduce the proportion of representation from those prairie co-operative grain companies; they have to go a step further. When they got down to the point of adding producer representatives, they made it very clear that they did not want anyone who had anything at all to do with prairie Wheat Pools to be part of that committee by way of being producer representatives.
Or the United Grain Growers; be fair.
That is right. I do not know whom we have got.

We would have got farmers.
September 29, 1983

The Elon. Member says it would have been farmers, but they would have been a very special kind of farmer. They would have been farmers who did not have anything to do with the local committees of the United Grain Growers or the various Wheat Pools. By placing them outside without ability to take part in this committee, you are eliminating a great many farmers in western Canada. I do not know the figures for Manitoba and Alberta, but I know from my own Province of Saskatchewan that there are approximately 800 Wheat Pool Committees made up of some 12 to 20 farmers each. Given a legal opinion and the reading of the resolution as it is now, all of those will be eliminated from being able to participate as representatives on the Senior Grain Transportation Committee. You are eliminating 15,000 or 16,000 farmers in Saskatchewan alone.
Not true.

1 have not even made allowance for the committee members who are part of the UGG structure. The history of the Wheat Pool movement is perhaps not well understood on this side. I do not know how they could forget, but the Wheat Pools and farmers are very closely allied, always were and always will be. I remind the House that the Wheat Pool movement began in my riding with some individuals from the Kelvington and Ituna areas who pushed to begin signing up people for the Wheat Pool which was finally begun in 1924, with a president from Bankend, again in that little triangle.
The membership is very much involved in the marketing of wheat pool grain. That was the reason they started. They started with at least 50 per cent of the grain signed up and committed to a five-year contract, a commitment which continues to this day. In our Province the pools have over 60 per cent of the business and they do not get that kind of commitment without having the full support of the Wheat Pool Committee members and individual members out on the farm.
I think no one with that kind of involvement in his community activities, including the marketing of grain and the interest he would have in being part of the local Wheat Pool Committee, should be eliminated from taking part as member of the Senior Grain Transportation Committee. Those are the very kinds of people we want on that committee. The legislation proposed by the Hon. Member for Kindersley-Lloydminster and amended by the Hon. Member for Red Deer prevents them from taking part.
Wrong.

I think it was a misinterpretation of what Members of Parliament are suppose to be doing here, a misinterpretation of the input individual members have within their organizations. The way this motion is written it would even prohibit a person who was part of a co-operative farm. To be a member you have to be a director in most of the co-operative farms I have in my area, and those people could not take part, simply because of the kind-

Mr. Speaker, 1 was in the process of pointing out the very clear connection between the grass roots farmers and their Wheat Pools. Some Members of the House were concerned that these farmers might not be represented on the Transportation Committee, and were therefore defending their position of ensuring that anyone who is a member of a

September 29, 1983
Western Grain Transportation Act
co-operative or corporation must not be allowed to be included in that committee. Farmers who have taken an interest in marketing grain have done so, to a very large extent, through the Wheat Pool movement by becoming members of the pool as young farmers and participating in local Wheat Pool Committees which are comprised of 12 to 20 people. Some of them are even larger than that. At each elevator delivery point, there is a Wheat Pool Committee with a chairman and a secretary. With the Bill as it is now worded, thanks to the amendment of the Hon. Member for Kindersley-Lloydminster, these people would be denied the privilege of participating as advisers and representatives on the Senior Grain Transportation Committee with which this Clause of the Bill deals. This is where the potential leadership for the farm movement originates, almost without exception. It is not doing anything for the agricultural movement in western Canada to try deliberately to eliminate these kinds of people from taking part as elected or appointed representatives of their organizations.
We think that this whole debate shows a bit of hypocrisy on the part of the Conservative Members, since they had the exact same clause in the original Bill as they are now attempting to put back in. They eliminated it themselves.
They repented.

Now I am pleased to see that they have repented. There have been a great many repentances on the part of that Party. The Conservatives fought a very weak fight at second reading. Halfway or two-thirds of the way through the committee stage, they decided that perhaps the NDP was right and that perhaps they should be opposing the Bill with a little more power and a little more influence than they had before.
Tell us about Mission-Port Moody.

At second reading, we heard barely one Conservative for every New Democrat who spoke. The normal process is three to one. They could not disturb themselves to take part in the debate at that time. I am pleased to see today that they have been stirred up enough to keep their usual share of the debate going and that they now find that the original way in which the Bill was written was fine. I hope they will be able to convince their Liberal friends again, as they did in committee, that a mistake has been made. I hope that we will be able to get this part of the Bill back to where it will be of some use to farmers so that farmers, who are members of the co-operative movement, either the United Grain Growers or the pools, will be eligible to be part of the Senior Grain Transportation Committee.

Mr. Speaker, it is always a delight to follow the Members of the NDP, because when they speak of hypocrisy, they just reflect it themselves. They are always so sanctimonious in their comments. They purport to represent the ordinary producer, yet they voted against Clause 3(c) which would provide for four active producers. The facts speak for themselves. One can look at the record. They purport to represent the senior people, the
labouring classes of the country, yet what do they do? They keep a Government in power that goes into deficit so far that the people who are hurt are the senior citizens, the poor people who can never get out. It is because the NDP keeps the Government in power.

Mr. Speaker, then the Hon. Member went on to another point. 1 think the truth of the matter is that Members of the NDP are speaking for the body corporate of the Wheat Pools, which are huge organizations. They have the vast majority of grain sales in the West. They are speaking for the body corporate, not for the little man who owns them. However, are they prepared to apply the Combines Investigation Act to them? No way. They are prepared to see the corporations getting 100 per cent of the market. However, concerning a newspaper or something that has 20 per cent of the market, they are prepared to attack it viciously, if an oil company happens to be a little larger, they will attack it viciously, but not the corporation.
The Hon. Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse) said that the reason the membership was reduced and the PC moved the amendment was that the Wheat Pools acted as one corporate body on the issue. The Hon. Member himself said that they always acted together, and therefore, why would they be given three votes? Would the Hon. Member be prepared to give Cargill three if it split itself into Cargill Manitoba, Cargill Saskatchewan and Cargill Alberta? Would he give the United Grain Producers three votes if it split itself into UGG Manitoba, UGG Saskatchewan and UGG Alberta? Of course it just has one vote because it has one legitimate interest. Of course, that is where the Minister and the Government made their largest mistake, when they went from the Gilson proposals which, concerning the method of payment, was 81 to 19, to what the former Minister of Transport then proposed, which was 50-50. By listening to the Wheat Pools, the body corporate, and giving it more power and legitimacy than it deserved, the Government acted as if it were representing all the farmers, but it was not. It represented the corporate interest. It was its duty. If I were the president or the director of the Alberta Wheat Pool and went up to a meeting, I would act for the corporation. That would be my job. I would be a director of the corporation. Therefore, the Government should have been seen in that light. The Government should not give the weight to the corporate interest that it did. It acted in unanimity, together, when it went into Quebec. It acted in unanimity when it came in and said, "Take off the active producers and put on only our three body corporates."
Take off, eh?

We simply would not agree with it. We felt that the interest of the man on the soil was different from that
September 29, 1983

of the corporate body, whether UGG, Cargill or the Wheat Pool.
The Wheat Pool, as a body corporate, has become very large. It has professional management, directors and the whole body. It is just as unrepresentative of the man on the soil as other corporations such as Esso. The NDP Members constantly rise to attack large corporations because they have a professional management body, but the Wheat Pools are no different.
Therefore, 1 stand in favour of the motion and 1 hope the Government will accept it. I have no doubt at all that the people of Canada will see through the NDP arguments purporting to represent and protect people and that they are actually injuring the very people whom they purport to represent.

Western Grain Transportation Act
the amendment 1 am speaking to very slowly so that the Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse) will be able to keep track of it.
At the outset I will say that the Hon. Member for Hum-boldt-Lake Centre did participate during several days as a member of the standing committee. Since the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) was in briefly to make a statement one afternoon and, for some reason, we did not see him again at all the remaining sittings we had throughout Canada, 1 can understand the mistakes and misinterpretations he made concerning this amendment. I would like to review for the House what occurred with Part 1 dealing with the Senior Grain Transportation Committee. At the outset, we who travelled with the committee across western Canada heard from approximately 20 Wheat Pool Committees that appeared before the Standing Committee on Transport. They said time and again that they were not sure that the Wheat Pool speaks for them. They indicated that they were not convinced that the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool, for instance, is representing them in a fair and open manner. They believed it might be tinged by some bias it has as directors for members of the corporate board. Therefore they wanted to express their views to the Members of the Standing Committee on Transport in the House of Commons and not those of the directors and officers of the company. They did so on several occasions.
We then had a submission made to us on behalf of the Canadian Co-Operative Wheat Producers Organization, which is an umbrella group for the Alberta Pool, Saskatchewan Pool and Manitoba Pool. When we examine the original Bill as it was first presented to the House by the previous Minister of Transport, we see that it provided for three representatives from the three pools. There was a representative from the United Grain Growers and a shared representation from what could be considered Richardson or Pioneer and Cargill Grain. The pools considered that to be a very large and cumbersome committee, as stated in their brief to the standing committee on behalf of the Canadian Co-Operative Wheat Producers Organization. They said they did not want to have those three men or women, who actively earned their livelihood from month to month and day to day by producing grain representing them but that the elected chairman of the Canadian Wheat Board Advisory Committee should represent all the producers in the three prairie Provinces. The chairman is probably elected by a 35 per cent voter turnout and probably receives 25 per cent of the vote. Nevertheless, he is elected.
The pools then came and said that in order to protect the feed grain producers in the Maritimes, Quebec, Ontario and B.C. we should have the chairman of the Canadian Livestock Feed Board, who is not elected but appointed, on the board. The pools wanted him rather than three feed grain producers. It was obvious to people who studied that situation that it did

September 29, 1983
Western Grain Transportation Act
not allow representation from the Maritimes but only from Ontario, Quebec and British Columbia.
We put forward an amendment to reduce the size of the Senior Grain Transportation Committee to comply with the request of the pools since they said it was too large. We eliminated two pool representatives but said they could have one, because this committee is not really one where votes will count. It is not a committee where votes will be decided for or against but one where views can be expressed. We felt that they could be expressed on behalf of those pools by the Canadian Wheat Producers Organization. To counterbalance that, we said that the producers should have four members consisting of one from Alberta, one from Manitoba and two from Saskatchewan.
Furthermore, rather than the only person to protect the consumers of feed grains being someone from the Canadian Livestock Feed Board, we suggested having one user of feed grains from the prairie basin, the three prairie Provinces. That made a lot of sense and was supported by members who wished to have producer representation.
As these hearings progressed we wanted to make sure that there was not a vested interest or duplication of interest in the expression of views on the Senior Grain Transportation Committee. Therefore, we took steps similar to those we take when we prescribe the ability to vote in a federal or provincial election in Canada. We enunciated the eligibility of those who could run in an election, such as we do for elections to this House or to legislatures across the country.

original Bill said. It negates the Conservative amendment introduced in committee on which the Liberals and Conservatives voted together. I have the records here.
When the sessions started at 9.40 a.m. on Thursday, September 1, the Hon. Member for Kindersley-Lloydminster (Mr. McKnight) moved the major amendment, "that Clause 3 be amended by deleting lines 11 to 39 on page 3 and lines 1 to 17 on page 4 and substituting the following therefor". What follows is close to what we have now. There were some further subamendments, for example, at 11.12, the Hon. Member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers) moved a further refinement to Clause 3(e)(i).
The Bill before us today is a combination of Liberals and Conservatives voting together to reduce the number of delegates from the Wheat Pool on the Senior Grain Transportation Committee. That is clear. Regardless of what the Hon. Members for Bow River (Mr. Taylor), Assiniboia and Kindersley-Lloydminster had to say, the truth is here and it is substantiated in the records. It was their amendment which reduced the number of representatives from the Wheat Pool from three to one.
In the debates today we heard justification of that original amendment introduced by the Conservative Party how the Wheat Pool, indeed, is one organization. As I listened to the speakers and read through the transcripts of the original debate, it was as though these Members were arguing the cause that they were arguing on Thursday, September 1. The arguments that many of them presented today were indeed the same type of argument that they were presenting on September 1. It is as though they are still arguing the cause that the pool should, in fact, have only one representative and not three.
I wish these Members would have heard the speech of my dear friend from Assiniboia who laid out the new line today. It is quite different from the line laid out on Thursday, September 1. The new line today, as it is in Motion No. 27, is to go back to what was in the original Bill. The line today is to support what the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) was saying in committee on September 1.
The line today is never to admit that you made a mistake. The Conservative Party can never admit that it made a mistake. It will not admit it made a mistake on September 1. Instead of admitting this basic mistake, it is totally changing direction from September 1 to today. They are now trying to bring in a group of red herrings: how often the Member for Yorkton-Melville attended the committee meetings, questioning the personal motivation of Members, shouting down our Members and trying to do everything possible except to admit that they have changed direction totally.
What they are proposing today and urging this House to accept is what they were arguing against on September 1. That is the simple truth. As the Canadian public listens to this debate, I hope they will not be influenced by the catcalling and all the red herrings from the Members on my right, but will realize one simple fact, that what the Conservative Party is proposing today was what they were opposing on September 1.
Western Grain Transportation Act
Today is September 29. That was on September 21. In 28 days we have seen a major turnaround. Why? I suspect that when it was finally realized what the Conservative amendments on September 1 did, the farming members in Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba started ringing their Members of Parliament and saying, "Are you guys crazy? Do you realize what you guys have done? You have totally emasculated the ability of the Wheat Pool to represent or make representations to this committee. You have reduced them from three to one."
The Conservative Party suggests that the Liberals always rule by poll. It is quite right. I might also suggest that today the Conservative Party enunciates its positions according to polls. It realizes that the producers in western Canada were totally outraged at the amendments it forced through committee, supported by the Liberals, and now it is desperately trying to backtrack from that position.
Unless we live in 1984 in the George Orwellian world-and we have not reached that yet-the record stands. Hon. Members interested in the topic can refer to the transcript of the committee hearings. They can go back to Thursday, September 1 and they will realize the greater mess into which the Conservative amendment put the producers of western Canada. It made a terrible Bill even worse. If the aim of the Progressive Conservative Party was to make a terrible Bill so obnoxious that no one could support it, indeed with its amendment on September 1 it moved in that direction. I think the Conservatives were surprised to learn that the Government would go ahead with the legislation and that their obnoxious amendment would be written in stone, included in the legislation and become a reality. They desperately want to backtrack from their position but, when they backtrack, they must clothe the issue in some good rhetoric-"we want to see more producers; we want freedom". The Conservatives have misused the term "freedom". Historians will shake their heads in shame. It has been a total misuse and abuse of the word.
Of course they are suggesting that the pools are like any other corporation and that they are not co-operatives. Sometimes one has criticisms about Wheat Pools as one has criticisms of all organizations, particularly democratic ones. There is no doubt that the Wheat Pools are representative of their members. I see Mr. Speaker indicating that my time is up. I wonder whether, with the unanimous consent of the House, I might have just another minute to conclude my remarks.
No.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: There does not appear to be unanimous consent.
What Tory said, "No"?

Mr. Speaker, did 1 hear you correctly that there was not unanimous consent? According to the established custom we have given consent to Conservative speakers to wind up their remarks.
