Western Grain Transportation Act

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Chair heard a negative voice in reply to the request for unanimous consent.
It is very surprising.
Mr. Speaker, just to set the record straight, I did not hear any "no" from our side.
It was from your side.
Yes, it was.

Certainly we were prepared to listen to the Hon. Member. It is always interesting to listen to people making fools of themselves. If he had continued, I would have had no objection. It is very interesting to listen to the comments of this great grain farmer from Regina East. He talked about producers, representing producers, and what was in their best interests. I did not hear any NDP Members say whether or not they were in favour of additional producer representation on the Senior Grain Transportation Committee. I did not hear any of them talk about what that committee would do. Those Members did not see fit to support the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) in his "Lone Ranger" vigilance before the Standing Committee on Transport. Now they are instant experts and want to talk about everything in the Bill. They want to explain the intricacies of the amendments and everything that occurred on September 1.
Where was the Hon. Member for Regina East (Mr. de Jong) on September 1 ? I do not think he was working as hard as the Hon. Member for Regina West or the rest of us who worked on the Transport Committee. Had he attended the hearings, he might have had a better idea of what those of us who attended went through regularly.
Stop attacking people and address the issue.

I hear him shouting and hollering and catcalling. That was the very thing he was blaming Hon. Members on this side for doing. I have with me a Canadian Wheat Board permit book. I wonder how many permit books the Hon. Member for Regina East has had in his long career as a farmer. That is the nub of the issue.
That is an old line.

I do not understand why he is shouting and hollering. He made mention of the fact that when people become excited and shout, it is because a nerve was struck. If he is as good at his word as he is with his lungs, what I am saying must offend him and have some validity. I wonder how much grain he has produced. I wonder what kind of a feel he has for producers. I wonder how many line-ups he has had the privilege of standing in on a hot day, trying to deliver grain at the end of a crop year. These are the kinds of things producers understand. These are the kinds of things which many of us in the Official Opposition have done in terms of farming, trying to stay in business and meeting commitments to our bankers or
business people who gave us credit. These are the kinds of things the Official Opposition attempted to represent.
In many ways the Bill was drafted in favour of the railways. Our main purpose on the Transport Committee was to get some amendments through which would in fact favour producers. 1 would be interested in knowing whether or not NDP Members were against additional producer representation. I did not hear them bemoan that fact. Why are they so strangely silent? Are they against producers, as the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) pointed out? Producers are really the foundation of the whole system. Without producers producing grain, we would not need the Bill, the Senior Grain Transportation Committee or all the things we will discuss in days ahead.
NDP Members talked about red herrings. I submit that this whole issue is nothing more than a red herring for them because they did not once address the substantive issue of what in fact the Senior Grain Transportation Committee would do. For the benefit of the NDP Members who did not attend the committee meetings this summer and fall, 1 will attempt to clue them in. It may be tough because I think it is very difficult to explain things to some of them. Basically the Senior Grain Transportation Committee will function as a group comprised of the various sectors involved in grain. Certainly the producer is the primary one, but it will also include elevator companies, shippers, people who handle grain on the coast, truckers, railway companies, elevator operators and terminal operators. This committee should function with all those participants at the table. It is important to have them all there. That is why this Party saw fit to include producers. Without producers, who are the first in the chain of production, we would really miss a very important link.
In addition, I would argue that producers have a basic, common sense understanding of what goes on. They are basically mechanics. They are able to farm because they understand machinery and they know about the grade of grains. They know what is involved in terms of cleaning and shipping grain of the same grade on unit trains to get away from shipping carloads of different grain and to get away from some of the switching at the terminals.
What does that have to do with the amendments before the House?

Producers have a lot of common sense and a basic understanding of the grain handling system. Some of the witnesses who appeared before the committee this summer thought there was no room for bona fide producers on the Senior Grain Transportation Committee. We were successful in moving an amendment to have additional producer representation on the committee. It was interesting that the Hon. Member for Regina East bemoaned that fact, but my Party moved an amendment which actually provided for an additional producer representative from his own Province. I would be interested to know if he was against that. Four producers will be elected: one from Manitoba, two from Saskatchewan and one from Alberta. I wonder whether the Hon. Member wants
September 29, 1 983

to shout, hoot, make noises and raise red herrings about that. At the moment he is strangely silent.
Returning to the Senior Grain Transportation Committee, it should involve all those factions so that problems can be settled at the table or in the room so that people do not go elsewhere to point fingers, blame someone else or raise false concerns in the press. There would be a chance to address issues right in the room.
Certainly there is concern about the size of that committee. Any of us who have been involved in committee work know the interesting saying that the best committee in terms of size is one of three with two absent. That goes a little too far, but if the amendment of the Hon. Member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gustafson) is accepted, I believe the committee will have 21 members. It will be a very large committee. Therefore, it is very important that the committee be structured properly, that the meetings be well organized, that the people who are to attend the meeting will have a chance to look at an agenda beforehand, will be well prepared, will know what the problem is and how it will be addressed and will proceed in that very businesslike fashion. Although we agree that a committee of that size can be rather cumbersome, I think there are ways for that committee to organize itself so that it will function and function well.
I also think that it is important for producers to be involved, Mr. Speaker, and that was essentially our feelings in committee. I point out to the Hon. Member for Regina East that I represent a rural riding that consists largely of farming communities. I do not think there are many farmers in Regina East, but in my travels to my constituency every weekend, I did not see that any producers were outraged. I did not receive any phone calls from producers who were upset that additional producers were to become members of the Senior Grain Transportation Committee. I do not know who members of the NDP were talking to, but my experience, Mr. Speaker, was not like their experience.
The Hon. Member said that it was a terrible Bill. In many ways, it is a terrible Bill. I believe that the Government itself realizes that the Bill has some shortcomings. The Government has indicated that by moving an amendment to establish review processes which would immediately begin looking at the Bill once it is passed.
I would agree with the Hon. Member for Regina East who said that the Bill is in many ways a flawed Bill, but I do not understand why members of the NDP did not take the opportunity of this amendment to raise some of the things that they think are wrong with the Bill and point out to the Government why they think it is terrible and where it can be improved. All we have heard from them is a tirade by these instant experts who did not see fit to attend any of the committee meetings. They abandoned the Hon. Member for Regina West and left him to do that very important job on the Transport Committee by himself all summer.
Western Grain Transportation Act
I do not particularly want to prolong this debate, but I would like to raise a point that may or may not be significant regarding its procedure. If this amendment is accepted, there should be a consequential amendment moved at the bottom of page 3 that would allow for the addition of the three members as moved by the Hon. Member for Assiniboia. That consequential amendment would raise the number of members on the Senior Grain Transportation Committee from II to 14. I assume that if the Government is prepared to accept this amendment, that will be taken care of, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I too am happy to be afforded the opportunity to make a few remarks on this first day of debate of the Crow freight rate Bill. Without a doubt, this is a historic day in the House of Commons. It is a day that Canadians have been talking about, thinking about and asking questions about for a long time.
I am very happy to see that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Axworthy) has been present through the whole debate today. I respect his presence although, with all due respect to my friend, the Hon. Minister, I would have to say that when I heard that he had been removed from the role of Minister of Employment, a very difficult role, and placed in the role of Minister of Transport in order to bring the Crow debate to western Canada, I could not help but think of the poem entitled "The Charge of the Light Brigade". I could see the Minister swashbuckling along in his cavalry uniform, with his helmet, sabre and pistol, on his horse and saddle as he heard the order: "Charge for the guns". If this Bill is passed and the Crow rate is changed, the Minister will be as flat on the ground politically as those 600 poor cavalrymen who rode against the guns. I think that he is probably well aware of that, so I will not continue with that line of thinking any longer.
It is true that we are participating in a historic debate today. During the preliminary discussions, there have been many friendly interventions between the Parties.
I am a western Canadian from the Prairies who grew up on a farm. I grew up within the system of co-ops and pools that are very much part and parcel of Canadian life in the West. From the time I was small, I knew that the things that were important in life were grain elevators, schools, churches and the like. I also knew, from listening to my father and my uncles and others, about the great difficulty that Canadian farmers had with handling their grain in the beginning.
I heard this summer that an amendment had been moved during the committee hearings. I give full credit to all Members of the House who sat through those committee hearings because they were long, hard and complicated and were held during a very hot summer. I have much respect for the people from all Parties who sat in on those hearings. Because of the work of those Members, we have before us what might be called the tracks of that committee. The committee's reports speak about the discussions and debate that occurred, about the people who were interested and presented statements and position papers to the committee. I must say that when I heard that the Wheat Pools would have only one representative on the Senior Grain Transportation Committee representing

September 29, 1983
Western Grain Transportation Act Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, realizing that the Wheat Pools still handle the majority of grain sales in the West, I was very surprised. I was surprised because it seemed to me to be a very unfair way of handling that particular situation.
The pools that handle the largest amount of grain sales in the West were built upon a historic way of handling grain that began when our fathers and grandfathers realized that they were not going to be able to cope with the big grain companies. They built their own pools, which afforded them a democratic, co-operative way of looking after themselves. I think that that must be greatly respected. I have a feeling that Members of the House have that respect, but when I heard that an amendment had been moved that would limit the three pools to one representative rather than three, I was shocked.
1 would like to point out that it is extremely important for Members who are participating in the debate but who were not present at the committee hearings to go over the reports of the committee hearings because much of the debate has been handled in those reports. From his remarks this afternoon, I would say that the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor), for whom ! have much respect, should do a little bit of reading. He should read the reports of the committee because I felt that some of his remarks did not, in my opinion, properly indicate the historic development of the amendments.
1 would repeat again that I have great respect for the parliamentary form of the Hon. Member for Bow River. I know that he is an outdoorsman and has done a great deal of good work with young people. He knows very well that one cannot cover one's tracks in the snow. 1 would suggest that the tracks made by the committee in preparation for today's debate are contained in the minutes of the committee hearings. I would suggest to the Hon. Member that he go and check those tracks, because I felt that he was unconsciously offering the House information that was not contained in the minutes.
1 was surprised by the remarks made by my good friend, the Hon. Member for Kindersley-Lloydminster (Mr. McKnight). From his remarks I understood he was suggesting that it was more important to have somebody represent views than represent votes on the Senior Grain Transportation Committee that will be established by the new Act. I personally believe that views are extremely important, naturally, and every sector should have its views properly represented. But when it comes to the crunch, 1 think everyone in the House and most people in the democratic process in Canada, realize that votes finally make the decision. I insist that the three pools be represented on the Senior Grain Transportation Committee because, in the final analysis, it will be extremely important that they have voting rights so that they can put their views into the democratic process.
During the debate this afternoon the tone of some of the remarks by my colleagues to my right spoke against the notion of co-operation, the basic notions that set up the co-ops and the pool systems and that one vote be represented in those
organizations and that they are basically different in their structure, philosophy and the way they operate from the grain companies.
I suggest that the Hon. Member for Lethbridge-Foothills (Mr. Thacker) should check his remarks. When he spoke I heard a tone that I think was condescending toward most of the grain farmers I know. He was almost attacking the people that this Bill is all about. It is important in the debate today and in the days following that we show respect for people on the farm.
Regarding the pools and their representation, 1 feel that the three prairie Provinces, a great wheat producing area of the world, should be represented by a member from each of the pools on the Senior Grain Transportation Committee.
I see that my time has come to an end, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak on this Bill. I am rather surprised that no Liberal Members have spoken on any of the amendments since they supported all the Tory amendments in committee. It is rather interesting that they are not willing to speak on the Bill now.
I should like to begin with a reference to my own constituency on Vancouver Island, a reference which may not seem to be too well related to the Bill but really it is. Some nine years ago I visited some retired prairie farmers who then lived in my riding. I noticed that in their homes plaques were exhibited in celebration of the fiftieth anniversary of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool which, as my hon. friend from Saskatchewan pointed out, was founded in 1924. They had a great feeling for their Wheat Pool because it represented them as basic, grass roots farmers. It was their organization and it represented a degree of emancipation from the elevator owners who had ripped them off for years. They were very proud to be members of the Wheat Pool and so the plaques had a prominent place in their homes.
I think it is significant that when the Bill was before committee the precise wording that Motion No. 27 is trying to introduce, was there. The Hon. Member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gustafson) is now trying to restore it but the Hon. Member for Kindersley-Lloydminster (Mr. McKnight) had changed that. I think it is very important that we recognize the importance of Wheat Pool members and the contribution they have made to farming in Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba. They should have proper representation on the Senior Grain Transportation Committee. This is a committee that will be responsible for making basic representations concerning the allocation of freight cars, and recommendations about how the system will operate.
It is interesting to note that some 60 per cent of grain shipped from the prairies comes from the three Wheat Pools, 17 per cent from the grain growers and about 20 per cent from the private organizations-about 20 per cent from the United Grain Growers and about 20 per cent from private organizations. The New Democratic Party suggests and it seems reasonable to me, that because some 60 per cent was being
September 29, 1983

shipped through the pools they should have three representatives on the committee, one from each of the prairie pools, the United Grain Growers, which shipped between 17 per cent and 20 per cent, should have a representative, and the private elevator companies, which ship about 20 per cent, should have a representative. That would make five representatives in all.
On the other hand, the Conservatives say that the three pools, which ship come 60 per cent of the grain, should have one representative, and the United Grain Growers should have one representative, making two from the total co-operative sector which accounts for 80 per cent of the total shipments. They add a representative from the private sector. We see where the Conservatives stand. It is interesting that they are now trying to repair some of that damage and changing their positions. This is typical of their approach to the Crow. They now say they are opposed to any changes for three years. We would like to see something more than this flip-flop policy. We would like to know where they stand.
I urge that the amendments put forward by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) be accepted. All Members paid tribute to his sterling work on that committee. This proposed committee should be made much more representative than it is as a result of the Conservative-Liberal coalition which stripped the pools of their proper representation.

Mr. Speaker, perhaps before I address my remarks specifically to the amendments I could express my sincere appreciation to Members of the Standing Committee on Transport who have spent a good part of the summer on this Bill.
Hear, hear!

One of my staff travelled with them, and in his last gasping moments before he expired at the end of the committee hearings he indicated to me that the committee met for 31 days over the summer and heard over 240 witnesses. That is quite a remarkable tour de force on the part of the committee. I believe the fact that we had well over 80 amendments moved by the committee and accepted, is also an indication that the work was not in vain but in fact produced an improved piece of legislation.
It is in that spirit, Mr. Speaker, that I would like to address the series of representations being made today. At the first opportunity I had to meet with that committee, as the new Minister of Transport responsible for this Bill, I indicated quite clearly that because of the very extensive debate which had taken place, and the representations which had been heard concerning membership of the Senior Grain Transportation Committee, that was a set of proposals which I was prepared to accept as a committee recommendation. Speaking on behalf of the Government, we were not taking a hard and fast line that it was something which was Government policy. We felt that that was something which should reflect the best wisdom which could be accumulating during the course of the commit-
Western Grain Transportation Act
tee hearings. It was in that spirit that our own Members supported the initial motion to reduce the number of members on the Senior Grain Transportation Committee.
I am interested to know, Mr. Speaker, that we now have a change in that position. It is a change which I personally welcome. Coming from western Canada I share many of the same sentiments which have been expressed during the course of debate, and 1 feel that representation of the producer groups is a very important element to have on the Senior Grain Transportation Committee. I share the notion that that committee is a central component of the whole change which we are introducing. It is the first time we will bring together all the different players in the game who will have to share information, knowledge, and also begin to share some responsibility for making the new system work. There will be the producers, the railways, the terminal companies and the truckers, all now sitting around the same table on a regular basis, and if they go back to some good old fashioned labour/man-agement procedures, they will realize that if you get all the parties in the same game sitting on a continuous basis, then the likelihood of an agreement is much higher. Furthermore, we might achieve a higher rate of efficiency in the system because each of the major players will have an opportunity to realize that he has an obligation and responsibility to get the best price for the farmers and the best cost in the system.
We sometimes tend to make the mistake of assuming that the delivery system of grain is purely railways. It is not. There are a number of other major players. Certainly, the terminals and the companies which gather the grain, the ports themselves, and the other forms of transportation, are all part of that linkage which comes together. In this particular committee we will have all those people having to get into that kind of discussion and, I believe, out of that will emerge degrees of consensus about the improved implementation of the grain delivery system in western Canada.
In saying that, Mr. Speaker, I want to indicate that we are quite prepared to accept the proposals put forward by the Hon. Member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gustafson). We think that the wording has a familiar ring to it, back to the original proposal. I do feel it is an improvement, frankly. Therefore, we can indicate to the Hon. Members of both Parties opposite that, if they are prepared to agree, we would also, as the Government, be prepared to go along and support that amendment.
I believe it was the Hon. Member for Portage-Marquette (Mr. Mayer) who pointed out that in order to make that amendment effective a series of consequential amendments would have to be moved, and it is the responsibility of the Minister to do so. I indicate to you, Mr. Speaker, that I am prepared to move those consequential amendments which would give force and life to that particular amendment. If it is in order to do so now, I would be prepared to do so. However, I notice that in the Speaker's instructions this morning, she indicated she wanted to have grouped amendments debated first and that we would be voting on them at a later date. I am really in the Speaker's hands as to whether I should move the

September 29, 1983
Western Grain Transportation Act
consequential amendments now or simply wait until those amendments are about to be voted on.
Perhaps there is agreement on Motion No. 27. I heard the Hon. Members of the New Democratic caucus saying they felt that producers should be involved. Certainly the movers of the amendment are in agreement. We are in agreement with it as well. Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, we could have this amendment accepted on this first day and then we can go on to other business. If that is the case, I would be prepared to move the consequential amendments along with it. However, Mr. Speaker, I will take your advice on how we might proceed.

Agreed.

Agreed.

Mr. Speaker, as I was saying, I have been very impressed this afternoon by the thoughtful contribution of Members of my caucus to this particular debate-

speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext: You are easily impressed.

-and the passionate pleas made by Members of my caucus on behalf of the farmers in the prairie Provinces. Those pleas arise I believe because of their deep concern that the measure before the House will destroy the co-operative spirit which has traditionally been a part of prairie life. As I understand it from both the minutes of the proceedings in the committee and the debate, at least from the Conservative side of the House, the only co-operative spirit which exists around this amendment exists in the coalition of the Conservative and Government Parties. I would also add that since some of my colleagues in the Conservative Party have been loudly boasting and bragging about how they are going to form the Government after the next election, I think they are going to be in for a big surprise in the prairie Provinces.
This is a prairie expert speaking here.

You will probably find that even though the Liberal Party does not exist west of Winnipeg, perhaps the Conservative Party will find itself in much the same position in certain sections of the western Provinces. I can understand why some of those Conservative Members would get rather excited about that because, contrary to the claims they have continually attempted to put forward that the NDP is somehow associated with the Liberals, surely the actions of the Conservative Party, both in committee and particularly on this amendment, clearly show to anyone who cares to look or listen that the true picture is that the Conservative Party is in the pocket of the Liberal Party. This particular amendment clearly eliminates any doubt which ever existed about any kind of allegiance they might expect from the farming community in this country.
It is not only a person like me who comes from the east end of Toronto, Mr. Speaker, who is particularly concerned about what this proposal is going to do to farmers. We in the cities appreciate that there has been a strong tradition of support in our country for farmers. We welcome and appreciate the contribution that the farming community makes to Canadian life. There are many people in my own constituency who came off the farms and who have spoken to me personally about their concern over what this Government is trying to do to the Crow rate, particularly the attitude this particular amendment displays towards the farmer and their importance in our community, their own local communities, the agricultural community generally, and particularly to the life of Canada.

September 29, 1983
Western Grain Transportation Act Surely, as Members of my caucus have expressed it in the past, in this debate and specifically this afternoon, the amendment, if passed, would be clearly undemocratic. It would make this particular Bill even more undemocratic than it was before it went to committee. It is not only myself nor the NDP that makes this statement. The Toronto Star, which one would hardly call a progressive paper in terms of where the NDP stands, published an editorial not too long ago which absolutely castigated the Government for what it was doing to the Canadian farmers. I would like to quote just a few paragraphs because I am sure that Members on all sides of the House will be quite interested. The Toronto Star stated:
Despite the opposition of provincial governments and of virtually every responsible farm group on the prairies, the federal government intends to unilaterally and drastically restructure the Crowsnest Pass Agreement. And if the Crow dies, the funerals of many western communities may follow.
It then goes on to state, "When the national Government- on our behalf', and with the words "on our behalf', it means not only Canadians who live on the Prairies but also others who have supported the farming community over the years, including those who live in cities, as 1 do, in the east end of Toronto. The Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism (Mr. Smith) asked of me in the past when I rose to debate this Government measure on the Crowsnest Pass rate, "Why is the guy from the east end of Toronto standing up to debate this issue"? The reasons I stand up are exactly the same reasons the Toronto Star put forth as to why Canadians should be concerned, why they should support the farming community regardless of where one lives in Canada. It is because the farming community is such a strong element in our traditional life and certainly in the economic life of this country. It is with that concern that the Toronto Star goes on to state:
When the national Government-on our behalf-proposes to disregard so cavalierly the deepfelt and legitimate concerns of one of our regions, all Canadians have cause to be disturbed. Our Confederation is based on recognition of the frequent need to subordinate local, parochial concerns to the broader national interests in which we all share; but it is equally based on recognizing the need for fairness, understanding and sensitivity in handling the legitimate claims and grievances of Canadians in all parts of the country.
This amendment clearly does not fall within the sense of understanding, fairness or sensitivity of the Star or any Canadian. Frankly, it goes beyond Canadians' view of Canada as being a fair country which does not believe in dealing meanly or unfairly with any part or constituency within the country.
The Toronto Star goes on to state:
As Western Canada sees it, the Crow is part of a Confederation bargain: Western Canada got low, fixed freight rates in return for agreeing to pay high import tariffs protecting eastern industries.
Residents of eastern Canada understand that they enjoy support from the farming community, and they were willing to enter into this bargain with the farmers in western Canada. The article continues:
Since then, the Crow's fixed rate-a half cent per ton-mile-has allowed our western farmers to compete for exports, from their land-locked position, with the
transportation-subsidized farmers of Argentina, Australia and the U.S. Grain is Canada's fourth largest export, accounting for sales last year of about $6 billion.
But the West's commitment to the Crow is based on concerns much deeper than simply cheap rates.
Mr. Speaker, I see that my allotted time has expired.
Continue.
With the agreement of the House, of course, 1 could continue speaking for another half hour about the injustice of this particular Bill. I will end on that note.

Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure, as the Hon. Member for Dauphin-Swan River, to register some of the concerns of my constituents over this particular Bill and the reason we are supportive of the amendment as brought forward by my colleague. The purpose of the amendment would be to eliminate from line 35 the word "co-operative". That is extremely important, especially in areas of the West, because members of co-operatives would no longer be excluded. The wording in the Bill as it is at the present time is very anti-democratic because it would mean that farmers at the grass roots level who were interested in participating in committees such as the Senior Grain Transport Committee would be excluded.
For the benefit of the House, may I mention the importance of co-operative tradition to western Canada. In fact, it is the grass roots involvement in co-operatives that has seen the rise of many people in western Canada with regard to their participation in our institutions in general. It is the co-operative spirit and the co-operatives themselves that have built up much of western Canada.
As I am sure the Minister of Transport (Mr. Axworthy) is well aware because of his roots in the West and his involvement at the University of Winnipeg in matters relating to people working together, it would be very unfair to have this type of wording in a clause which would prohibit participation by those farmers at the grass roots level who have been and are involved in co-operatives. I am very pleased that before the amendment was even brought before the committee, a Member of our Party was the one who stood up for the rights of individual members who are members of the co-ops. This particular wording underlines the lack of understanding of the drafters of the Bill concerning the unique way in which the farming culture has developed in western Canada.
For that reason, it is important to see that we adopt the amendment brought forward by my colleague, as it recognizes the fact that it is the co-operative spirit that has built up the West. I would therefore urge Hon. Members to support this particular motion.

subtopic: SHIPBUILDING-PIP GRANTS-LOSS OF JOBS IN SHIPYARDS. (B) CONSTRUCTION OF DRILLING RIGS

speakerposition: Deputy Opposition Whip; Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: SHIPBUILDING-PIP GRANTS-LOSS OF JOBS IN SHIPYARDS. (B) CONSTRUCTION OF DRILLING RIGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on a number of occasions I have risen in the Chamber to express some concern that continuation of the Petroleum Incentive Program grants established by this present Government would in fact negate or perhaps totally obliterate the few positive aspects that were contained in the Government's assistance to shipbuilding last January or February.
As recently as September 20, I brought the plight as seen by the Canadian shipbuilding industry and its related industrial framework to the attention of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde). Their concern is that unless the Government takes steps to maximize Canadian content flowing from PIP grants, the impact on Canadian industry will be very bad indeed.
The reason for raising the question again stems not necessarily from the growing concern by all sides of the Chamber, I am sure, but by the industry as well, that we now have virtually a $7 billion tiger by the tail. No one quite knows how to control it. In fact, the grants are beyond the power of this House to deal with other than by cutting them off and I do not believe anyone is suggesting that. I am looking for a clear and concise answer about the Government's intention with respect to the impact that the program has on the Canadian shipbuilding industry in its present from.
In just the last six months the Canadian industry is down by some 6,000 jobs. That makes a total of approximately 12,000 jobs which have been lost in the last 18 months. The reason for that loss is that, according to the PIPs program, capital costs are not included. Therefore it is to the advantage of the entrepreneur to have someone else build an offshore service rig or a drilling platform and then lease it from him because the cost of leases can be included in the 80 per cent grant toward this type of energy exploration and development.
It would be one thing if the entrepreneur went to a Canadian shipyard and told it to build a structure, lease it back to the entrepreneur who would then pay the shipyard. If that were the case, we would be providing and stimulating Canadian employment in our shipyards and support industries in that sector of our economy. What happens, however, is that it is cheaper-when the entrepreneur sees that he cannot get access up to the 80 per cent grant, since he will pay a certain amount more if he builds a rig in Canada-to go off shore to Korea, Japan, Norway or another country to build it. He can get the advantage of cheap financing through Export Development. Since his responsibility is to his shareholders and he is not in
Adjournment Debate
the business of losing money for his investors, he goes offshore to find a foreign builder and then leases the rig back. He then brings it back into the country under a foreign flag. It does not need a Canadian crew and only has to meet a minimum-not Canadian-standard with respect to operation in our coastal or northern areas. That is what happens first.
To demonstrate that, PetroCan, in the first blush of Canadian nationalism, built several offshore service rigs in Canada. The incentives grants came in. Petro-Canada said that it was being silly by continuing to use its own ships. Therefore, it sold them offshore, or wherever it could sell them, and then leased them back. It charged this country with 80 per cent of the total cost that was allowable. In fact, it included the full cost of the lease, not just 80 per cent.
The spin-off is that what happened will continue to happen because when you bring a foreign vessel into this country, a duty must be paid. Lo and behold, we find that the 80 per cent grant pays for importing the ship. This is therefore a good thing for the entrepreneur.
While the grants are good in terms of stimulating new energy development in this country, they deprive Canadian workers of sustainable long-term jobs. This shows up in the figures and indicates why Canadian shipyards are facing the worst year in the last 15. I invite the Parliamentary Secretary to enlighten us as to whether the Government intends to bring in some modifications to change these one or two narrow points.

speakeroldname: Mr. Douglas Fisher (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: SHIPBUILDING-PIP GRANTS-LOSS OF JOBS IN SHIPYARDS. (B) CONSTRUCTION OF DRILLING RIGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the PIP grants are providing up to 80 per cent for exploration in the offshore and 25 per cent for development costs in the offshore. However, when a grant is given, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Chretien) has the power to supervise plans for the employment of Canadians and for the full development of opportunities on behalf of Canadian manufacturers and suppliers. In addition, under a grant there is the right of the office of Regional and Industrial Benefits in the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce to review plans to ensure that these opportunities are being given to Canadians.
Hon. Members will notice that I use the word "opportunity". I do not say that these two different ministries have a dictatorial power. We cannot provide a dictatorial power because of our obligations under GATT and because market conditions and the intelligent operation of these companies require that they must have some outside option beside Canadian suppliers.
There is a balancing act here. No doubt we would all like to see the exploration and development activities in the offshore, plus 100 per cent of supply, undertaken by Canadian companies and Canadian shipyards. However, under GATT we cannot demand that 100 per cent of the supply take place in Canadian shipyards. We do not have that power under our international obligations.

September 29, 1983
Adjournment Debate
Unfortunately, the Hon. Member does not get all his facts entirely straight. The losses that he describes are not as a result of PIP grant incentives but a result of an enormous world glut in exploration equipment. Second, it is as a result of the recent general slowdown in ship purchases all over the world.
It would only be fair for the Hon. Member to note that government activity has more than offset much of this slowdown. In fact, government activity is specifically designed for that. The $700 million coast guard ship acquisition and refurbishing plan under the special recovery program is intended to speed up activity in the shipyards, to take projects that were further down the line and schedule them for today.
We believe that the patrol frigate given to the Saint John Shipbuilding and Dry Dock Co. Ltd. will offset much of this slowdown. The new regulations, customs jurisdiction, temporary extension of subsidies to Canadian shipbuilders and the adoption of new coastal trading rules combine to provide some offset to this world glut of equipment and to the general slowdown that the industry has experienced.

subtopic: INDUSTRY-WHITE FARM EQUIPMENT LTD.-URGENCY OF ISSUE
INDUSTRY-WHITE FARM EQUIPMENT LTD.-URGENCY OF ISSUE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 want to raise an issue this evening which 1 raised in the form of a supplementary question this afternoon in the House. I very much appreciate being on the adjournment debate list, because this is the type of thing for which the adjournment debate should be used.
Earlier I asked the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism (Mr. Smith) a question concerning the situation of White Equipment. It is a well-known issue of which most farmers are aware because the White Farm and the Cockshutt names in farm equipment have long been associated with agriculture in Canada and throughout the world.
The imminent problem is that at nine o'clock tomorrow morning it is my understanding that the court-appointed receiver, Peat Marwick, will determine what will happen to the company. One of my concerns is that there are many people who will be affected by the move tomorrow morning. It relates to jobs, both direct ones at the plant in Brantford and those with dealers across the country.
It is my information that there are 123 dealers in Canada. The majority of them are in Saskatchewan, according to my information there are approximately 50 in that Province. As far as jobs with the dealers are concerned, I would estimate that there are roughly ten jobs per dealer. That would be a conservative estimate. There could very well be more. My guess is that we are talking of something in the order of 1,200 to 1,500 jobs in the dealership network across Canada. At the peak of the operation of White Farm Equipment, it employed something like 1,100 people. Even if we took a figure of 500 people at the plant, we would be talking in the neighbourhood of 2,000 jobs. This is a significant number of jobs, especially when we will face a very tough winter as far as employment is
concerned. This issue does have consequences in respect of jobs.
The Government should also be concerned about the service end of the matter. As I said, the White Farm and Cockshutt names in farm equipment are synonymous and have long been associated with agriculture in the world. There are very major implications for farmers who have purchased this equipment. In addition to the 2,000 lost jobs I referred to earlier, this also involves an issue regarding service.
What will happen to the people who purchased expensive combines in the last two years or three years? Will they be able to obtain service? Will parts for these combines be available? What will happen to their resale value or their trade-in value on new equipment? There will be far-reaching consequence in terms of the individual farmers who are affected, and this comes at a time when farmers like everyone else are facing financial difficulty. Some people who have recently became involved in farming have purchased this equipment. 1 know of instances where this will cause extreme financial problems and in some cases could even be the determining factor in whether or not people are able to stay in business.
The issue also involves technology. I am a farmer. 1 have owned combines and I have operated Cockshutt combines. It is my understanding that the technology associated with the new 9700 model of White combine is extremely important because it performs very well in the field. There is an opportunity for Canadians to pursue this technology and to develop a name for themselves outside the country. 1 know there are many White combines across the line in the United States. I would suggest that we also have an export potential if we can maintain this operation and technology in Canada.
This issue has consequences in four areas: in jobs, in service, in technology and in our ability to export, and that relates to our balance of payments, interest rates, the value of our money and all those things.
Let me quote from the Regina Leader-Post of September 20, 1983:
The court-appointment receiver-Peat Marwick Ltd.-is looking for a buyer who will protect the jobs at the Brantford plant as well as the dealers and the axial-flow combine technology developed by White with federal financial help, Lumley said.
It has come to my attention in the last couple of days that a group in Winnipeg is prepared to put forward a very serious bid that would save the company and keep it from being liquidated. The members of that group are concerned that they may not have enough time to meet the nine o'clock deadline tomorrow morning. Let me indicate what I am asking from the Government. I know my time is fast running out, Mr. Speaker.
The people from Winnipeg who are involved in this offer are, I understand, in the farm equipment manufacturing business. They are putting together an offer that will include the dealers, which means that the dealers themselves will be putting up some money. I think it is very healthy for them to be involved directly. They are, however, concerned that they
September 29, 1983

may not have enough time to meet the nine o'clock deadline tomorrow.
1 know that the Government itself cannot legally interfere with the actions of the receiver. However, 1 am suggesting that the Government use every method it can to see that this legitimate group from Winnipeg has the time to make its offer to the court-appointed receiver tomorrow morning. If there is a chance to save these jobs, to provide this service to farmers and do the things that the Minister himself said he hoped to do, we should in fact provide enough time for this offer to be made tomorrow morning. I would ask again that the parliamentary secretary address this problem and use whatever influence he has with the Minister to see that in fact this offer from Winnipeg has a chance to materialize in time to be of some use to the receiver.

Mr. Speaker, I can understand the concerns of the Hon. Member for Portage-Marquette (Mr. Mayer), because it is true that we are talking about thousands of jobs, about preserving the dealer network and about preserving the technology involved in this situation.
The Hon. Member knows that the Minister and the people involved in ITC, as well as the receiver, have been trying to find somebody that would continue to operate White Farm Equipment Ltd. of Brantford in a viable way. subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-NUCLEAR TECHNOLOGY-POSSIBLE EXCHANGES BETWEEN ARGENTINA AND LIBYA. (B) RELATIONS WITH ARGENTINA
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-NUCLEAR TECHNOLOGY-POSSIBLE EXCHANGES BETWEEN ARGENTINA AND LIBYA. (B) RELATIONS WITH ARGENTINA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I make this intervention in the Adjournment Debate this evening subsequent to a question that was asked on June 2 of this year of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen). That question was prompted by two things; the Falklands crisis, and the press reports which indicated that the Argentinian Government was negotiating with Libya for nuclear materials. That report indicated that the nuclear materials might in fact have been medical isotopes, but there was no confidence that the relationship between Libya and Argentina would be held at that level.
The concern I expressed at that time to the Minister was that Canada inadvertently, through the relationship we had established with the sale of the Candu reactor to Argentina
Adjournment Debate
and through the ongoing supply of uranium fuel to Argentina, was an unwitting accomplice to the possible proliferation of nuclear weapons materials. Well before the question of the Falklands crisis, our relationship with Argentina was and has continued to be a tenuous one. Argentina has refused to sign bilateral agreements which we felt were important to make sure that Canada's involvement was not in the field of nuclear weaponry. It is true that Argentina had signed agreements with us, but the bilateral agreement that is important to us now, and those subsequent to the unfortunate history of the Candu sales in the East, were not forthcoming from the Argentinian Government. We know that Argentina has been reprocessing fuel since our sale of the Candu reactor to Argentina. It now has plutonium in quantities large enough to produce bombs.
With the report that Argentina was negotiating Khadafy I think there was a great level of concern around the world that we would see the birth of another member of the nuclear weapon family. Several coincidences have occurred in this past week. The first was that Margaret Thatcher while here reminded us of the type of Government there is in Argentina, and that it is unreliable. In addition, recent press reports on the memoirs of Richard Nixon indicate that he has said that Khadafy used to give him nightmares. If the general can do that to Richard Nixon then I suggest we ought to pay attention to him.
The question I should like to leave with the Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs is whether we in Canada have any additional information on this. In spite of the fact that I fully support the entire nuclear system, I should like to know whether we have taken a good solid look at withdrawing from our relationship with Argentina because of present difficulties, and those that may occur in the future if we continue to co-operate with Argentina.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean Lapierre (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-NUCLEAR TECHNOLOGY-POSSIBLE EXCHANGES BETWEEN ARGENTINA AND LIBYA. (B) RELATIONS WITH ARGENTINA
speechtext:
As everyone knows, Mr. Speaker, Canada and Argentina have just completed together a Candu-type nuclear station at Embalse. The station was officially opened on May 3, 1983 and has now come on stream. However, such industrial cooperation for peaceful use of nuclear technology falls within the four corners of the January 1976 bilateral nuclear cooperation agreement between the Canadian and Argentinian Governments. As it has been stated on several occasions in the House, this agreement is altogether consistent with Canada's December 1974 non-proliferation policy which was aimed at ensuring to the fullest extent possible that Canadian nuclear materials would not encourage proliferation.
In December 1976, the Government of Canada changed its policy so as to make sure that our nuclear trade would involve exclusively such countries as those which were formally committed through the Non-Proliferation Treaty or a similar
27606

September 29, 1983
Adjournment Debate
agreement to reject nuclear explosive technology and to put all their nuclear facilities under international guarantees. Rather than putting an end to the existing and fruitful cooperation with Argentina, the Government decided at the time that our cooperation would not extend beyond the Embalse project for as long as the Argentinians would not agree to the provisions of December 1976.
As far as I know, Mr. Speaker, the Argentinian Government has steadfastly denied having any intention of developing nuclear weapons. On the other hand, everything leads me to believe that, in its relations with other countries, Argentina is prudent and moderate. The fact remains that states are sovereign and free to choose their nuclear partners. Should Argentina want to cooperate with Libya, surely it will keep in mind the fact that that country is signatory to the Non-Proliferation Treaty and that all its facilities are controlled by the International Atomic Energy Agency.
Any planned diversion of nuclear matters or Canadian technology to Third World countries must be agreed to in advance by our country. The Canada-Argentina agreement is perfectly clear on this. We have no reason to believe that the Argentina government wishes to divert some items of Canadian origin without the consent of our government, something it agreed freely not to do on signing the agreement in January 1976. Some have also alluded to a possible trade between Argentina and China. Anyone interested in this issue, including the hon. member, will be happy to learn that the government of China applied for membership in the International Atomic Energy Commission on September 6, and that its representatives have indicated publicly on many occasions that they want to avoid the proliferation of nuclear weapons.
